$comment: The curated half of the DOM binding: what AngleSharp's attributes cannot say. Every entry carries a
reason, and every entry has to name something the pinned assemblies actually have — DomBindingsOverrideTests
fails on one that does not, so this table can never quietly describe a version of AngleSharp nobody
references any more. Members left out for a reason the generator worked out for itself (a Task-returning
member, a delegate parameter, a type the conversion table has no entry for) are NOT listed here: they are
in the generated report, with the reason the generator gave.

excludedInterfaces.reason: Window is the browser runtime's, not the binding's: the global object stays Jint's GlobalObject and gains Window.prototype in its chain (campaign item R1). Generating a second Window here would produce an interface object nothing could ever be an instance of. document.defaultView is skipped with it, by the conversion table rather than by name.

manual.reason: AngleSharp's IHtmlCollection<T> is generic and invariant, so a static member body cannot name the receiver type. item() and namedItem() are hand-written against DomCollectionBase's two virtuals instead, and the interface contributes no members to any closure — its refinements inherit them through the prototype chain, which is where a browser has them too.

skip.reason: HTML's `add((HTMLOptionElement or HTMLOptGroupElement) element, ...)` is a union, and AngleSharp models it as two AddOption overloads sharing one [DomName]. The generator binds one member per name, so one half would always lose; re-declared in `additions` over a body that dispatches on the argument's interface.
The same union on the collection, and the same two overloads.

DOM requires a SyntaxError DOMException for a selector that cannot be parsed, and a page has to be able to catch it -- jQuery's own support detection asks for `:has(*,:jqfake)` inside a try. AngleSharp raises a CLR AngleSharp.Dom.DomException instead, which walks through a script's catch and out of the page loop, and AngleSharp.Css NREs outright on that input. Re-declared in `additions` over the same AngleSharp call, wrapped so that the failure is the DOMException the standard names.

Activation behaviour: a click is a dispatched event with a default action, not a method call on the element. AngleSharp's DoClick dispatches on AngleSharp's own event bus and runs no activation behaviour at all — a checkbox it clicks does not toggle. The events bridge re-declares click() in `additions`.
Focus is a document-level concept. AngleSharp's DoFocus does not set IDocument.ActiveElement, so its focus() would move nothing. The events bridge re-declares focus() in `additions`.
The other half of focus(), re-declared in `additions` for the same reason.

Form reset fires a cancelable reset event whose default action resets the controls; AngleSharp's Reset() is only the default action's second half and fires nothing. The events bridge re-declares reset() in `additions` and calls AngleSharp's Reset() from it.

AngleSharp never assigns IDocument.ActiveElement — not on DoFocus, not on parse — so the generated accessor answers null for the whole life of a document, where HTML says the body element. The events bridge owns focus and re-declares activeElement in `additions`.

Skipped rather than re-declared: the inherited DOMTokenList.value is already the standard's, so this interface is left with no members of its own, which is what the standard leaves it with too.

DOM §4.5 declares it as `boolean hasFeature()` -- no arguments at all, and the standard's own note says it is kept only so that legacy feature detection takes the modern path. AngleSharp answers false for 133 of the 136 pairs `DOMImplementation-hasFeature.html` asks about, and its first parameter is required, so `hasFeature()` was a TypeError as well. Re-declared in `additions` as the one line the algorithm is.

DOM §4.5's legacy creation surface, which the standard still requires and half the events corpus is written against. AngleSharp's own is skipped because it answers an AngleSharp Event; this builds the Jint event the alias names, with the empty type and the initialized flag unset that make it undispatchable until initEvent() has named it.

DOM §4.5. AngleSharp's IDocument has no member for it — a CDATA section lives in AngleSharp.Xml, which is not in the generator's pin — and its first step is a NotSupportedError on an HTML document, which is what dom/common.js catches and a missing member is not.

DOM §4.5.1. AngleSharp's IImplementation is createHTMLDocument, createDocumentType and hasFeature, and nothing else, so there is nothing to project; the algorithm is DOM's own over the pieces AngleSharp does have.

DOM §6.1. AngleSharp has it, but its third parameter is a NodeFilter delegate and the conversion table has no entry for a delegate — deliberately, because only the standard knows a callback's IDL shape. Dom/Views/NodeFilters accepts both shapes DOM's legacy callback interface allows.
DOM §6.1, and the same delegate parameter as createTreeWalker.
Selection API §3: document.getSelection() answers the same object window.getSelection() does. AngleSharp has no Selection at all, so the interface is the runtime's.
DOM §6.2 `readonly attribute NodeFilter? filter`. AngleSharp's ITreeWalker.Filter is the CLR delegate, which cannot cross back; the value the page passed is remembered at creation instead.
DOM §6.1, the same as TreeWalker.filter.
DOM §5.5 declares Range's stringifier. AngleSharp implements it as Range.ToString() and puts no [DomName] on it, so nothing in the metadata says the member exists.
CSSOM View extends Range with it and AngleSharp has no layout to answer from. Zeros, honestly, until the flat-box model (campaign item C4) gives every box a deterministic rectangle.
The other half of getBoundingClientRect: an empty list, because a range with no layout covers no boxes.

DOM §4.8 `readonly attribute ShadowRootMode mode`, and the member a page reads to tell an open root from a closed one. AngleSharp has IShadowRoot.Mode but puts no [DomName] on it — the only member of the interface without one — so nothing in the metadata says it is projected.
DOM §4.2.5. AngleSharp's [DomName] is getDistributedNodes, which is the Shadow DOM v0 spelling; both are emitted, because the old one is what the metadata says and the new one is what a page calls.
DOM §4.2.5, the element-only half of assignedNodes.

AngleSharp's DoClick is skipped because it dispatches on AngleSharp's own bus and runs no activation behaviour at all.
AngleSharp's DoFocus never assigns IDocument.ActiveElement, so its focus() would move nothing. FocusOptions' one member is preventScroll, which nothing here could honour or violate.
The other half of focus(), for the same reason.

AngleSharp has no visibility state at all - there is no IDocument member for it - and a page reads it to decide whether to animate, poll or reconnect. Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled is what moves it.

AngleSharp's [DomName("submit")] sits on SubmitAsync(), whose Task return has no conversion-table entry. HTML's submit() skips both the interactive validation and the submit event, which is the whole of what distinguishes it from requestSubmit().
AngleSharp has no such member at all; it is the one that behaves like a button, so the submit event fires and a listener can stop it.

Form reset fires a cancelable reset event whose default action resets the controls; AngleSharp's Reset() is only that default action and fires nothing, so it is called from the event half rather than projected.

DOM section 4.4's isConnected. AngleSharp's INode has no member for it at all, so there is nothing to project; every client library asks a node whether it is still in the document before it clicks it, and an absent member makes every element handle read as detached.

The flat box model (docs/design/headless-browser.md section 8): AngleSharp has no layout, so CSSOM View declares this member and nothing in the metadata can. Jint.Browser/Layout/FlatLayout answers it from tree order, and the same model answers DOM.getBoxModel and Input.dispatchMouseEvent, so a client that reads a box and clicks its centre gets one consistent story.
The other half of getBoundingClientRect: one rectangle for an element that has a box and none at all for one that does not, which is what a page testing getClientRects().length for visibility asks.
The padding box of the flat model, which for the scrolling element is the viewport.
The other half of clientWidth.
Zero: a flat box has no border for a client edge to measure.
Zero, for the same reason as clientTop.
Nothing overflows sideways - every box is exactly as wide as the viewport - so this is clientWidth.
The document's own height for the scrolling element, and the element's box for everything else: only the page scrolls here.
The page's virtual scroll offset, and the one metric that is writable: writing it on document.scrollingElement scrolls the page, and on anything else does nothing.
Zero, and a write changes nothing: there is no horizontal overflow to scroll.

The virtual scroll's other setter, and the one a client's own click path calls before it checks that a box is inside the viewport. Both argument forms are read - the legacy boolean and ScrollIntoViewOptions' block member.
The border box of the flat model, which has no border, so it is the box.
The other half of offsetWidth.
The distance from the offset parent in document coordinates, which is what distinguishes it from getBoundingClientRect().top: this one does not move when the page scrolls.
Zero: nothing is laid out horizontally.

Nothing here is positioned, so HTML's walk to the nearest positioned ancestor always ends at the body - which is what a browser answers for an unpositioned element. The body, the document element and an element with no box answer null, as they do in Chrome.

The flat model's hit test, which is the same one DOM.getNodeForLocation and a mouse event at a coordinate go through - so a client that clicks the centre of a box it read is told the same element was hit.
The hit element and every rendered ancestor above it, innermost first. Boxes nest exactly as the tree does in this model, so the list is the ancestor chain rather than a second hit test.
The one element whose scrollTop moves the window, which is how a client finds the page's own scroll offset. Standards mode always: it is the document element.

DOM 7's XPath, which neither pinned assembly declares: there is no [DomName("evaluate")] anywhere in AngleSharp, so nothing could generate it. The evaluator is System.Xml.XPath over AngleSharp.XPath's navigator - see Dom/Views/JsXPath. htmx 2 builds an XPathEvaluator at the top level of its bundle, so a page that loads it is a ReferenceError without this.
The compiling half of XPathEvaluatorBase, which a page reuses across evaluations the way htmx does.
Legacy, and DOM keeps it only because pages call it: its whole definition is now 'return the node'.

AngleSharp declares the handlers as CLR events, which the member closure never yields, and as member entries they would be a hundred and seventy near-identical rows; the extend form exists for exactly this.

DOM §7.1's stringifier, which the standard defines as `value`'s own steps: the attribute value verbatim, and the empty string when the attribute is absent.
DOM §7.1: the getter is get-an-attribute-value and the setter is set-an-attribute-value, both verbatim, so neither normalises. AngleSharp's ITokenList has no member for it at all.

That is a per-realm data slot, which the member form cannot say, because a member entry is an operation and an operation has a body.

hooks.reason: HTML 3.2.6: the script whose text is running. AngleSharp answers the head of its DEFERRED script queue, so it is null for exactly the case a page uses it in -- see the divergence table. It used to be an own property of the document wrapper because a getter could not be hooked.

HTML 3.1.6: the host advances it and fires readystatechange. Document.ReadyState's setter is protected, so nothing outside AngleSharp can move it and the parser driver's readiness is the only true one.

DOM 4.5: the document's URL, which pushState and a fragment navigation move without reloading. AngleSharp's document address cannot follow without raising its own Location.Changed navigation, so the page's URL is the answer.
DOM 4.5 gives documentURI the same value as URL, and it moves for the same reason.
HTML 3.1.5: the document this one was reached from, which only the navigator that reached it knows.

DOM 4.4: the node document's base URL. The <base href> is resolved against the PAGE's URL, so the answer moves with it; on Node rather than on Document because that is where DOM declares it, and where a browser answers it for every node.

HTML 3.1.6: the cookies of the document's URL, from the one jar every request of the browsing context reads and writes -- and with RFC 6265bis 5.5's HttpOnly rule applied, which AngleSharp's own document has no notion of.
The write half of the same jar.

DOM's create-an-element: with the synchronous custom elements flag set the element a defined name produces is the CONSTRUCTOR's and not AngleSharp's, so the answer belongs to the host. The hook's default runs the custom-element path and falls through to AngleSharp's own call when the document has no definition, which is what a binding with no registry behind it did before.
The namespaced half, which answers a plain element for every namespace but HTML's.
The same AngleSharp call, and then the upgrade DOM's clone steps enqueue -- so the node the page is handed is the host's answer rather than AngleSharp's.

Setting innerHTML parses markup into the tree, and a <script> inserted that way has to reach the script scheduler. Until the parser driver exists (campaign item R3) the hook's default body assigns AngleSharp's property directly, which is exactly today's behaviour; R3 replaces the body and nothing generated changes.
The same parse, replacing the element itself (campaign item R3).

HTML activates an event handler when its content attribute is set, and the listener it creates keeps its position among the addEventListener listeners for ever. This is the one write of an attribute the package can see, so it is where `onclick="…"` takes its place in the list; the hook's body is the AngleSharp call it replaced, plus that reconciliation.
The other half of setAttribute: removing a handler content attribute deactivates the handler, and the listener goes with it.
The same parse, at a position relative to the element (campaign item R3).
document.write during parsing writes into the live text source while the parser is parked, which only the parser driver can do (campaign item R3).
document.write with a newline appended (campaign item R3).

$reflectedComment: This is the one list whose entries come from the STANDARD rather than from AngleSharp. Every other list
in this file corrects what the pinned assemblies say; a row here states what HTML says about one
attribute -- which of the thirteen reflection algorithms it takes, its keywords, its invalid and missing
value defaults, its range -- none of which any CLR signature carries. A `long` and a `long` limited to
only non-negative numbers are the same Int32 property, and <col span> defaulting to 1 while <select size>
defaults to 0 is nowhere in the metadata at all.
An entry REPLACES the member AngleSharp projects under that name, which is the opposite of what
`additions` does and is deliberate: most reflected attributes are projected already, from a property that
hands back the raw attribute value or parses it with a different default. Neither the presence nor the
absence of the AngleSharp member is an error, so the generated report says which of the two each row was.
The type names are HTML's own, which are also the ones web-platform-tests' html/dom/reflection.js uses,
so a row can be read straight off the corpus table that tests it.

reflected.reason: HTML §3.2.6.4: `dir` is an enumerated attribute with an empty invalid and missing value default, so an unknown value reads back as "" and a known one in its canonical case. AngleSharp's Direction is the raw attribute, so `el.dir = '5%'` answered "5%" and `dir=LTR` answered "LTR".

HTML §3.2.6.2: `lang` reflects the content attribute and nothing else. AngleSharp's Language walks to the nearest ancestor that has the attribute and falls back to the current culture, so an element with no `lang` anywhere above it answered "en-US" -- a page asking what language THIS element declares was told what machine it was running on.

HTML §6.6.3: `tabIndex` is a reflected long, so HTML's rules for parsing integers decide it -- they take a prefix, which is why `tabindex="1.5"` is 1 and `tabindex="5%"` is 5 where AngleSharp answered 0 for both. The default stays 0 rather than HTML's -1-unless-inherently-focusable, which needs a focusability model this package does not have; Dom/AGENTS.md records it.

HTML §6.6.6 puts `autofocus` on HTMLElement, not on the form controls: AngleSharp declares it only on the elements HTML4 could focus, so `div.autofocus` was undefined and setting it made an expando that wrote no attribute.
HTML §6.8.5: an enumerated attribute of the ElementContentEditable mixin, which HTMLElement includes. AngleSharp has no member for it at all.
HTML §6.8.4: an enumerated attribute of the ElementContentEditable mixin, which HTMLElement includes. AngleSharp has no member for it at all.
HTML §16.2: an obsolete attribute the standard still requires the IDL attribute for. AngleSharp has no member for it.

HTML §4.12.1 reflects `src` AS A URL, so it answers the absolute URL the attribute resolves to against the element's node document. AngleSharp's Source is the raw attribute value, which is the divergence Dom/AGENTS.md recorded and the browser lane's html/webappapis/scripting/ rows were triaged against.
HTML §4.12.1: a boolean attribute AngleSharp has no member for, so `script.noModule` was undefined -- and a page feature-detecting module support reads exactly this.

HTML §2.6.7: a CORS settings attribute is an enumerated attribute whose IDL type is DOMString?, so an absent attribute is null and any unknown value -- including the empty string -- is the Anonymous state. AngleSharp handed back the raw value, so `crossorigin=""` answered "" where a browser answers "anonymous".
HTML §16.2: an obsolete attribute the standard still requires the IDL attribute for. AngleSharp has no member for it.
HTML §16.2: `htmlFor` reflects `for`, the one member of this group whose IDL name and content attribute name differ. AngleSharp has no member for it.
HTML §4.7.1: `cite` is reflected as a URL. AngleSharp's Citation is the raw attribute value, the same divergence script.src has.

HTML §4.7.1: `dateTime` is a plain reflected DOMString -- the value is a date string but the IDL attribute does not parse it. AngleSharp types it as a DateTime, so the conversion table had nothing to project it as and the member was absent.
HTML §16.2: an obsolete boolean attribute the standard still requires the IDL attribute for. AngleSharp has no member for it.

nullableStrings.reason: DOM §4.9: `DOMString? getAttribute(DOMString qualifiedName)` — null when the attribute is absent, and scripts test for it.
DOM §4.3.3: `readonly attribute DOMString? attributeName` — null for every record but an attributes one, which is how a callback tells the types apart without reading `type`.
DOM §4.3.3: `readonly attribute DOMString? attributeNamespace` — null for an attribute in no namespace, which is nearly all of them.

DOM §4.3.3: `readonly attribute DOMString? oldValue` — and null is load-bearing here, because it is also what an observer that did not ask for the old value must see. The empty string would be indistinguishable from an attribute whose previous value really was empty.
DOM §4.4: `attribute DOMString? nodeValue` — null for every node type but Attr, CharacterData and ProcessingInstruction.
DOM §4.4: `attribute DOMString? textContent` — null for a document and a doctype.

nullableParameters.reason: DOM §4.4: `Node insertBefore(Node node, Node? child)` — a null child appends, which is how every virtual DOM adds its last row. AngleSharp annotates the parameter nullable and implements it, but the emitter reads C# optionality rather than nullable-reference metadata, so the table is where WebIDL's nullability is stated.

nonNullableParameters.reason: DOM 4.9: `undefined setAttributeNS(DOMString? namespace, DOMString qualifiedName, DOMString value)` -- only the namespace is nullable. AngleSharp annotates the value nullable because its own setter reads null as removing the attribute, so without this row `setAttributeNS(ns, 'x', null)` would remove where a page is owed the string "null".
HTML 7.4.5: `undefined pushState(any data, DOMString unused, optional USVString? url = null)` -- the url is nullable and the second argument is not, however unused it is.
The other half of pushState, and the same signature.
HTML 4.11.4: `undefined close(optional DOMString returnValue)` -- non-nullable, so `dialog.close(null)` sets returnValue to "null" and the dialog's `returnValue` is a DOMString a page reads back.

HTML 4.12.5: `DOMString toDataURL(optional DOMString type, optional any quality)` -- non-nullable, so a null type is the unrecognized MIME type "null" and the answer falls back to image/png, rather than being read as no type at all.

HTML 4.8.11: `TextTrack addTextTrack(TextTrackKind kind, optional DOMString label = "", optional DOMString language = "")` -- both trailing arguments are non-nullable DOMStrings with an empty default.
The language half of addTextTrack, and the same clause.

HTML 4.10.19.3: `undefined setSelectionRange(unsigned long start, unsigned long end, optional DOMString direction)` -- non-nullable, and a direction the enumeration does not carry is "none" rather than an absent direction.
The textarea half of setSelectionRange, and the same clause.

add.reason: DOM §5.5 puts START_TO_START and its three siblings on Range, but AngleSharp only ever passes the enum as an argument to compareBoundaryPoints, so the returns-it rule does not find them.
